evaluation.positioning_hook: A washed-up jazz pianist in Lisbon is offered bunker salvation if he finishes one last song, but the woman who wakes him up may be the one thing he can’t buy his way into saving.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The apocalypse premise gives this immediate commercial shape, but the emotional engine is intimate and adult rather than broad four-quadrant. The strongest audience is prestige-drama and elevated-genre buyers who respond to romance, mortality, and a strong central performance role.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast: a pianist in a collapsing Lisbon bar is recruited by a bunker operator and must finish a song to earn survival. The premise is easy to explain in one breath and the ticking-clock structure is baked into the opening pages.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Morgan is built as a damaged, performative lead with a real contradiction: he’s emotionally sealed off, but his entire survival strategy depends on making people feel something. Marie, Michel, and George all have distinct behavioral signatures that give the script more than a single-hero engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a lush, music-driven apocalypse with a very specific sensory language: ticking watch, jazz standards, bunker luxury, and Lisbon decay. The choice to make the central conflict about art, preservation, and emotional surrender gives it a fresher lane than a standard end-of-the-world drama.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a clear engine and repeated escalations: the passport hunt, George’s leverage, Marie’s push-pull, and the final choice. It does slow into extended romantic and philosophical passages, but the ticking clock and recurring reversals keep it moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s core idea feels both novel and inevitable: a musician bargaining with the end of the world while trying to decide whether survival without love is worth anything. The bunker-as-cage, song-as-soul, and watch-as-mortality metaphors are all cleanly integrated into the plot.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Lisbon feels lived-in and story-generating, with the hotel bar functioning as a pressure cooker for class, fear, barter, and performance. The bunker economy, passport lottery, and collapsing city give the world rules and hierarchy rather than just backdrop.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: This has a very distinct tonal identity: elegiac, romantic, and apocalyptic, but with a polished jazz-club sophistication rather than grim survivalism. The script knows exactly how it wants to feel, from the ticking watch to the candlelit bar to the final musical release.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing that the real subject is not the asteroid but Morgan’s fear of living, loving, and being seen. The bride memory, the watch, the unfinished song, and George’s collector mentality all suggest a deeper psychological and thematic layer beneath the surface plot.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Morgan/Marie carries the emotional center, but Michel and George give the room recurring friction and texture, and the hotel guests create a functioning pressure-cooker ensemble. It’s not a true ensemble piece, but the bar environment generates enough recurring relationship energy to support the feature.

lead_characters.name: Morgan Aireheart
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, white, American expatriate, professional musician/pianist.
lead_characters.hook: A brilliant but emotionally barricaded jazz pianist living in Lisbon, Morgan has the posture of a man who has already lost everything and is trying to survive by controlling the room. He’s carrying grief, a failed marriage, and a private unfinished composition called 'Stardust,' and the script keeps testing whether his talent is a gift, a defense mechanism, or both.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Oscar Isaac in Inside Llewyn Davis or Bradley Cooper in A Star Is Born — a musician role where performance, self-destruction, and vulnerability are inseparable. It gives an actor the chance to play restraint, romantic longing, and live musical authority in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Marie Freeling
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, white, American, emotionally resilient but vulnerable, multilingual or at least functional in Portuguese/French contexts.
lead_characters.hook: Marie enters as a bright, disruptive presence in a room full of resignation, but she’s not just the love interest; she’s the script’s moral counterweight and emotional truth-teller. She’s carrying her own grief, her own survival calculus, and a private refusal to be purchased by George’s bunker logic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Rebecca Ferguson in The Greatest Showman or Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman a chance to control the temperature of every scene they entered. It offers an actor a rare blend of warmth, steel, romantic chemistry, and a late-story emotional pivot.

lead_characters.name: George Drier
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 60s, white, affluent, controlled, likely American or international elite.
lead_characters.hook: George is the film’s quiet predator: immaculate, patient, and terrifyingly practical, a man who treats art, people, and survival as assets to be curated. He never needs to raise his voice because the threat is in his composure; he’s the kind of antagonist who makes every room feel owned.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Ralph Fiennes in The Grand Budapest Hotel or Michael Shannon in Take Shelter its pleasure: precision, menace, and intelligence without overt villainy. It’s a prestige antagonist part with real scene-stealing authority.

lead_characters.name: Michel
lead_characters.hook: Michel is the film’s grounded witness, a man who has already made peace with the end and therefore has more dignity than anyone else in the room. He’s dry, observant, and quietly philosophical, with a bartender’s instinct for what people need before they know they need it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that lets an actor do what Richard Jenkins did in The Visitor or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom — calm authority, lived-in sadness, and understated emotional weight. It’s a delicious character part with memorable lines and real humanity.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, glamorous, socially agile, likely local or expatriate, emotionally compromised.
lead_characters.hook: Ava is a survivor who uses charm, appetite, and social intelligence as currency in a collapsing world. She’s flirtatious, wounded, and opportunistic, but the script keeps letting her reveal the panic underneath the polish.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the sharp, volatile showcase of Jennifer Jason Leigh in The Hateful Eight or Juno Temple in Fargo. It’s a compact but juicy part with bite, vanity, and vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Markus
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, unstable, physically compromised, likely local or expatriate.
lead_characters.hook: Markus is the fragile hinge of the early plot: a friend, a liability, and a human bargaining chip whose body and secrets drive the first major turn. He’s not built for longevity, which is exactly why the script uses him so effectively.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable role that gives an actor a fast, high-impact turn like the early-casualty parts in The Departed or The Place Beyond the Pines. It’s a pressure-cooker role with immediate stakes.

lead_characters.name: Nadia
lead_characters.hook: Nadia is the story’s innocence under siege, but she’s not passive; she watches everything, absorbs the room’s moral weather, and becomes a quiet test of who still deserves saving. Her presence sharpens the film’s emotional stakes without ever feeling ornamental.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor the emotional precision of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project or Brooklynn Prince-style vulnerability with real narrative consequence. It’s a small but meaningful part that can make a lasting impression.

lead_characters.name: Azar
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, desperate, likely immigrant or traveler, father/husband.
lead_characters.hook: Azar is one of the film’s clearest faces of the passport economy: a father trying to convert everything he owns into a chance for his family to live. He’s a pressure valve for the world-building and a reminder that the apocalypse has already become a market.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a heartbreaking, lived-in turn like Barkhad Abdi in Captain Phillips or Shohreh Aghdashloo in House of Sand and Fog. It’s brief, urgent, and emotionally legible.

lead_characters.name: Cyra
lead_characters.hook: Cyra is the maternal counterpoint to the film’s survival calculus, a woman trying to keep her family intact while the world monetizes their fear. She’s less about plot mechanics than about the human cost of every bargain in the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do concentrated emotional work in a few scenes, similar to the mother roles in Room or Minari. It’s a compact grief-and-protection part with real resonance.

lead_characters.name: Victor Reis
lead_characters.hook: Victor is another face of the bunker class: cultured, compromised, and visibly aware that he’s participating in a system that will not save everyone. He adds a second layer of artistic competition and social hierarchy around George’s operation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a sharp, uneasy supporting turn like Stanley Tucci in The Lovely Bones or David Strathairn in Good Night, and Good Luck. It’s a polished, tension-filled part with status and ambiguity.

lead_characters.name: Elias
lead_characters.hook: Elias is the keeper of memory in a world that’s liquidating itself, a man who refuses to trade away the last meaningful object in his store. He gives the film one of its cleanest moral statements: not everything can be priced, even at the end.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran actor do the quiet moral authority of Hal Holbrook in Into the Wild or John Hurt in The Proposition. It’s brief, elegant, and emotionally exact.

lead_characters.name: Mrs. Gable
lead_characters.hook: Mrs. Gable is a comic-pressure release with teeth, the kind of old-world survivor who has no patience for apocalypse theatrics. She punctures the room’s self-importance and makes the hotel feel inhabited rather than staged.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun, scene-stealing character part in the tradition of June Squibb in Nebraska or Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey. It gives an older actor a sharp comic beat with real attitude.

lead_characters.name: Gideon
lead_characters.hook: Gideon is the film’s quick-hit embodiment of predatory privilege, a man who assumes access and ownership even as the world collapses around him. He exists to show how little the apocalypse has changed certain men.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact antagonistic role that lets an actor play entitlement with menace, like a smaller-scale version of the rich men in Saltburn or The White Lotus. It’s brief but sharply defined.

casting_characteristics: One teen role (Nadia) with sustained emotional presence
One strong musical lead who must plausibly perform piano and carry singing/playback moments
Several 40s-70s supporting roles with specific age texture
Multilingual or accent-sensitive supporting casting for Lisbon setting

notable_requirements: City street exteriors with collapse/riot texture

technical.vfx_details: Asteroid imagery, city-wide atmospheric collapse, dream/space inserts, and impact-night environmental enhancement; mostly selective rather than constant.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical destruction, broken glass, riot texture, body handling, and atmospheric lighting/sound design.

rights_flags.detail: NATO is repeatedly named as the bunker/passport authority in the premise.
The Blue Note is specifically named as a performance venue.
Long Island is specifically named as a drink order, but not a clearance issue on its own.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige theatrical, awards-leaning specialty, or premium streaming original

budget.note: Contemporary Lisbon, a contained hotel/bar core, and limited stunt demands keep this in range, but asteroid VFX, riot texture, night exteriors, and impact-night atmosphere will push above a barebones indie if not scoped carefully.

casting.note: The lead needs an actor who can credibly play jazz piano, carry romantic chemistry, and sustain interior grief across the whole film; Marie also needs a performer who can sing, spar, and hold the emotional counterweight.

development.note: The script’s emotional and philosophical material is strong, but the bunker bargain, Marie’s final choice, and the ending’s moral resolution will be the main pressure points in buyer conversations.

comp_set.title: The Fountain
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the same elevated, metaphysical romance DNA and the same willingness to make love, mortality, and cosmic imagery carry the emotional load.

comp_set.title: A Star Is Born
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it hinges on a musician lead, live-performance emotion, and a love story that doubles as a self-reckoning.

comp_set.title: Melancholia
comp_set.why_it_comps: The apocalypse is used as an emotional amplifier rather than just a disaster engine, with a similarly elegiac, end-of-the-world mood.

comp_set.title: The Last Black Man in San Francisco
comp_set.why_it_comps: It shares the lyrical, memory-soaked approach to place and the sense that the protagonist is trying to preserve something already slipping away.

comp_set.title: The Menu
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not in plot, but in the controlled, high-concept pressure-cooker of elite people trapped in a curated environment with escalating moral stakes.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige romance, elevated genre, and emotionally literate apocalypse stories with strong music and performance elements.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, slightly female-leaning, urban/educated audience, strong appeal to viewers who respond to character-driven, auteur-friendly genre films.

budget_tier.note: A contained contemporary feature with a limited number of principal locations, but the asteroid imagery, night exteriors, and crowd/riot atmosphere keep it above microbudget.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally with buyers who want a high-concept emotional hook without superhero scale: a contained, actor-forward feature with a clear visual identity and awards-friendly melancholy. The music performance element gives it a casting and marketing angle beyond a standard end-of-the-world drama.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is vivid, but there is no clean sequel or spinoff vector beyond this specific story.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the premise in one sentence, which makes it easy to package, pitch, and market without over-explaining the mythology. That clarity is especially valuable for streamer development teams and indie financiers looking for a clean elevator pitch.
strengths.evidence: Morgan is offered bunker salvation if he finishes a song while the world counts down to asteroid impact.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Morgan is a real actor role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead combines musical performance, emotional repression, romantic longing, and moral compromise, which is exactly the kind of part that can attract a serious name. That makes the project more attachable than a standard contained genre piece.
strengths.evidence: He plays live in the bar, hides behind a mask, and is forced to choose between survival and love.

strengths.what_it_means: Lisbon and the hotel/bar ecosystem create a contained pressure cooker with class, survival, and performance all colliding in one place. That gives the film a production-friendly world that still feels rich and cinematic.
strengths.evidence: The bar, corridor, rooftop, record store, and ruined streets all feed the same end-of-world economy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The music is story, not decoration.
strengths.what_it_means: Because the songs are tied to memory, identity, and the bunker bargain, the music can function as both emotional payoff and marketing asset. That opens the door to a soundtrack-forward campaign and a stronger audience memory than a standard drama.
strengths.evidence: The unfinished 'Stardust' composition becomes the emotional and structural spine of the film.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a clean, elegant villain with status, intelligence, and a believable power structure, which is valuable for both casting and audience retention. Buyers know how to sell a story when the antagonist is this controlled and specific.
strengths.evidence: George curates the bunker, controls access, and treats Morgan like an acquisition.

strengths.what_it_means: The final choice to reject the bunker bargain and play for the room gives the film a satisfying emotional release that can land with audiences and awards voters alike. That kind of ending helps the project feel complete rather than merely concept-driven.
strengths.evidence: Morgan leaves the car, returns to the bar, and turns the final performance into a communal act.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, actor-forward prestige genre feature with a clean hook, a distinctive musical identity, and a production footprint that stays inside indie-to-low-mid territory. The combination of an attachable lead role, a vivid Lisbon pressure-cooker, and a romance wrapped in apocalypse gives it real buyer appeal for streamer originals, specialty distributors, and prestige financiers.

items.area: The bunker bargain narrows the buyer pool.
items.detail: The premise is elegant, but the emotional and philosophical weight of the bunker deal means this is not a broad commercial apocalypse play. Buyers will see it as prestige-leaning, adult, and tone-sensitive rather than four-quadrant genre fare.

items.area: Morgan needs a very specific lead actor.
items.detail: The role asks for piano credibility, romantic chemistry, wounded interiority, and enough charisma to carry long stretches of silence and performance. That is a real casting lift, and the project’s value rises or falls with the attachment.

items.area: The ending depends on Marie’s final choice.
items.detail: The emotional resolution hinges on Marie refusing the bunker logic, then the film pivoting into communal catharsis. That’s a strong thematic move, but it is also the kind of ending that will be read carefully for plausibility and audience satisfaction.

items.area: The asteroid imagery adds cost pressure.
items.detail: Even though the film is mostly contained, the impact-night visuals, city-collapse atmosphere, and dream-space inserts will require selective VFX and strong sound design. It’s manageable, but not free, and the scope needs to be held in check.

items.area: The script leans hard on mood and repetition.
items.detail: The watch ticking, the jazz motifs, the mirror imagery, and the repeated bunker conversations create a strong signature, but they also risk feeling over-insistent if the buyer is looking for a leaner thriller engine. The film is most attractive to buyers who want tone and theme as much as plot.

issues.headline: The main friction is commercial positioning: this is a prestige, mood-forward apocalypse romance, not a broad disaster movie, and that will shape every buyer conversation. The other pressure points are casting the lead at the right level and keeping the VFX/impact-night scope disciplined enough to stay inside the indie lane.
